newsitem.title: USA: SABRE seen a slow performer in face of competition.
newsitem.headline: SABRE seen a slow performer in face of competition.

text.p: AMR Corp's long-awaited spin-off of about 16 percent of its SABRE Group Holdings Inc's unit will be well received, but SABRE's stock is expected to be a slow performer as the reservation and information systems company faces increasing competition.
"It's a fairly priced deal, but I don't see any major upside right away. The stock will be a slow performer," said Manish Shah, editor and publisher of the IPO Maven, who tracks new stock offerings.
The initial public offering is expected in early October.
SABRE's 20.2 million share offering is expected to price in the range of $20 to $23 a share, valuing the deal at about $434 million.
SABRE is the largest electronic distributor of travel data in the U.S. The unit also provides information technology solutions to the airline industry.

While the spin-off would allow SABRE to broaden its customer base, the company faces formidable competition from computer systems companies such as Electronic Data Systems Corp and Computer Sciences Corp.
More than half of SABRE's $1.5 billion in 1995 revenues came from reservation bookings made by travel agents, with the balance coming from its information systems services.
The constantly changing nature of the technology sector makes SABRE's future results less certain, analysts said.
"Since there's a lot of competition in those areas, it's difficult to project future earnings," said Brian Harris, an airline analyst with Lehman Brothers.
Once publicly traded, SABRE will be one of the 10 largest computer services companies in terms of market capitalization, the company said.
Harris said the offering values SABRE at about $2.56 billion to $2.94 billion, which is within the range of his estimates.
David Menlow, president of Springfield, N.J.-based IPO Financial Network Corp, said he expects SABRE to have an opening day premium of about 10 percent.
"Big name companies will be well received by the market. The offering will meet with some heavy institutional demand," Menlow said.
The proposed SABRE offering ends years of speculation about its fate.
In 1989, AMR explored merging SABRE with a similiar system owned by Delta Air Lines Inc, but the carriers abandoned those plans when faced with antitrust hurdles.
SABRE was also rumored to be an acquisition target of International Business Machines Corp, but both companies had declined to comment on the issue.
AMR may sell more of SABRE in the future, but some analysts said the offering will appease investors who have been clamoring for action, some airline analysts said.
Samuel Buttrick, an airline analyst with PaineWebber, said he expects AMR to retain control of SABRE "for the foreseeable future."
"But that does not preclude them from selling off additional holdings," Buttrick said.
The SABRE deal is expected to boost AMR's share appreciation, analysts said. On Monday, AMR's shares traded down 3/8 to close at 83-1/8 on the New York Stock Exchange.
